title: Fact, Opinion or Value?
objective: After this level you can sort a statement into a checkable fact, a personal taste or a value judgment.
summary: Factual claims can be checked by observation or research, even when wrong. Opinions of taste have no such check. Value judgments say what ought to be, against a standard.

cards.headline: Three claims about mice. Each one is checked in a different way.
cards.body: "Mice are animals." "Mice make the best pets." "You should feed your pet mouse every day." All three are claims in Level 3's sense. But you'd settle them very differently: one with a biology book, one probably never, and one by asking what we owe the animals we keep.

cards.fact: A factual claim can be checked by observation or research.
cards.context: "Mice are animals" is one. Logicians call such claims descriptive: they say what is in fact the case. A factual claim can also be wrong. "Mice are reptiles" is still a factual claim, just an erroneous one, and any biology book will set it straight.

cards.headline: Taste: no referee
cards.body: "Mice make the best pets" and "Blue is the best color" are opinions. The OpenStax textbook College Success defines an opinion as a statement someone holds to be true without supporting evidence. You can collect facts about mice all day, and a cat lover still won't be proved wrong.

cards.headline: Value judgments: measured against a standard
cards.body: "You should feed your pet mouse every day" is different again. It's a normative claim, or value judgment: it says what ought to be, measured against a standard, such as a moral or a legal one. Words like should, ought, good and bad are the giveaway. To weigh one, first ask which standard it appeals to.

cards.headline: Statements: sorted
learned: Factual claims can be checked, even when wrong
Opinions of taste have no evidence to settle them
Value judgments say what ought to be
Should, ought, good and bad signal values

questions.prompt: How can a factual claim be checked?

options.label: By how many people agree with it
By how confident the speaker sounds
It cannot be checked at all
options.rationale: Checkability is exactly what makes it factual.

questions.explanation: Factual claims can be verified through observation or research.

questions.prompt: Which word most often signals a value judgment?

options.label: Usually
options.rationale: "Usually" describes how often, a factual matter.

options.label: Because
options.rationale: "Because" introduces a reason, not a value.

options.label: Therefore
options.rationale: "Therefore" introduces a conclusion, not a value.

questions.explanation: Words like should, ought, good and bad signal a normative claim about what ought to be.

questions.prompt: "Mice are reptiles" is false. What kind of statement is it?

options.label: An opinion, because it is wrong
options.rationale: Being wrong doesn't turn a fact claim into an opinion.

options.label: A value judgment
options.rationale: It says nothing about what ought to be.

options.label: Not a claim at all
options.rationale: Level 3: a false sentence is still a claim.

options.label: A factual claim, just a wrong one

questions.explanation: It can be checked and found wrong, so it's a factual claim, just an erroneous one.
